Atomic Habits: The 1 Percent Rule: The 1 Percent Rule - British cycling had won one Olympic gold medal in nearly a century. Then Dave Brailsford took over.
Hide The Candy: Make It Obvious - Google wanted its employees to snack healthier, so it studied its own offices.
Say When And Where: Implementation Intention - Researchers split people into three groups to see who would exercise each week.
Habit Stacking: Habit Stacking - BJ Fogg, a Stanford researcher, wanted to build an exercise habit.
Habit Bundling: Temptation Bundling - Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania wanted people to go to the gym more.
The Two Minute Rule: The Two Minute Rule - Stephen Guise was tired of failing at big workout plans.
Never Miss Twice: Never Miss Twice - Researchers at University College London followed volunteers building a new daily habit.
Become The Type Of Person: Identity-Based Habits - Researchers asked some people, how important is it to you to vote.
Out Of Sight: Make It Invisible - Researchers at the University of Texas gave people tests that need focus.
Add Friction: Make It Hard - Streaming services figured out that people watch more when the next episode starts on its own.
Make It Satisfying: Make It Satisfying - Language app Duolingo uses a simple counter: how many days in a row you have practiced.
Don't Break The Chain: Habit Tracking - The story goes that Jerry Seinfeld told a young comic to write jokes every day.
Patience Pays: The Plateau Of Latent Potential - Warren Buffett began investing as a child, and for decades his wealth looked ordinary.
Join The Right Tribe: Join A Culture - The Framingham Heart Study followed thousands of people and tracked who they were connected to.
Wanting Beats Having: Craving Drives Action - Neuroscientist Wolfram Schultz watched monkey brains while they got a juice reward after a light.
A Tingle That Sold Toothpaste: Make It Satisfying - In the early 1900s hardly anyone brushed their teeth. Pepsodent changed that with a big ad campaign.
Everyone Else Is Doing It: Social Proof - Researchers tested signs asking hotel guests to reuse their towels.
Score Yourself Daily: Habit Scorecard - Benjamin Franklin picked thirteen virtues he wanted to build, like order and moderation.
Lock Away The Escape: A Commitment Device - Victor Hugo was far behind on his book and kept getting distracted.
Change The Scene: Context Triggers Habits - Around one in five American soldiers in Vietnam had used heroin, and experts feared a wave of addiction at home.
Peer Pressure Is Real: Conformity - Psychologist Solomon Asch showed people three lines and asked which matched a fourth.
The Checklist That Saved Lives: Make It Easy - Doctors at Johns Hopkins faced deadly infections from central lines in intensive care.
Point And Call: Make It Obvious - Train staff in Japan point at signals and say what they see out loud, like signal is green.
Pay For Your Habit: Motivation Fades - Economists studied thousands of gym members who chose monthly memberships.
Tech Disasters: The Rocket That Exploded: Integer Overflow - In 1996, Europe launched the Ariane 5 rocket on its very first flight.
Pounds Versus Newtons: Unit Mismatch - In 1999, NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter approached Mars and then vanished.
45 Minutes To Lose 440 Million: Failed Deployment - In 2012, Knight Capital deployed new trading software to its servers.
The Two Digit Year: Bad Date Assumptions - In the early days of computing, memory was expensive, so programs stored years as two digits.
A Machine That Overdosed Patients: Race Condition - The Therac 25 was a radiation therapy machine used in hospitals in the 1980s.
The Bug That Leaked The Internet: Missing Bounds Check - In 2014, a bug called Heartbleed was found in OpenSSL, software that secures much of the web.
The Binary Search Bug: Integer Overflow - Binary search looks simple, and for decades programmers wrote it the same way.
The Chip That Couldn't Divide: Lookup Table Error - In 1994, a mathematician found that Intel's new Pentium chip gave slightly wrong answers for some divisions.
The Rover That Kept Rebooting: Priority Inversion - In 1997, NASA's Mars Pathfinder landed and started sending back pictures.
A Clock That Drifted: Rounding Drift - During the 1991 Gulf War, a Patriot missile battery failed to intercept an incoming missile.
The Wrong Server Wipe: Untested Backups - In 2017, a GitLab engineer was fixing a database problem late at night.
A Pattern That Broke The Web: Catastrophic Backtracking - In 2019, Cloudflare pushed a new firewall rule to all its servers worldwide.
Eleven Lines That Broke Builds: Dependency Risk - In 2016, a developer pulled his packages from npm after a naming dispute.
The Plane That Ran Out Of Fuel: Unit Confusion - In 1983, an Air Canada Boeing 767 ran out of fuel in mid flight.
The Clock That Was 11 Hours Off: Bad Time Sync - In 2019, Boeing's Starliner capsule launched on a test flight to the space station.
The Day Facebook Vanished: Single Point Of Failure - In October 2021, Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp all went offline for about six hours.
The Leap Year Freeze: Date Edge Case - On December 31, 2008, Microsoft Zune players froze when they were switched on.
One Extra Line: Skipped Check - In 2014, Apple fixed a serious security flaw in iPhones and Macs.
The 49 Day Crash: Counter Overflow - Windows 95 would crash if it ran continuously for about 49 and a half days.
The 248 Day Bug: Counter Overflow - In 2015, aviation regulators warned that Boeing 787 generators could shut down if left powered on for too long.
A Typo That Broke The Internet: Unsafe Tooling - In 2017, an Amazon engineer ran a command to remove a few servers from a billing system.
Excel Renamed Human Genes: Silent Auto-Conversion - Excel automatically converts some text into dates, so the gene SEPT2 became the second of September.
Decision Bias: The Rigged Wheel: Anchoring - Psychologists Kahneman and Tversky spun a wheel rigged to stop on either ten or sixty five.
The Mug Experiment: The Endowment Effect - Researchers gave some students a coffee mug and asked others to bid for the same mug.
The Same Cure Described Two Ways: The Framing Effect - Tversky and Kahneman told people a disease threatened six hundred lives and offered two programs.
The Smoke And The Seizure: Diffusion Of Responsibility - Psychologists John Darley and Bibb Latané set up a staged emergency over an intercom.
The Obedience Experiment: Obedience To Authority - In 1961, Stanley Milgram told volunteers to give electric shocks to a stranger whenever he answered wrongly.
The 2 4 6 Puzzle: Confirmation Bias - Peter Wason showed people the numbers two, four, six and said they follow a rule.
The Invisible Gorilla: Inattentional Blindness - Researchers Simons and Chabris showed people a short video of teams passing basketballs.
24 Jams Or 6 Jams: Choice Overload - Researchers set up a tasting stand with twenty four jams, then another with only six.
One Word Changed The Whole Impression: The Halo Effect - Students were told a guest lecturer was either a rather warm person or a rather cold person, with everything else identical.
The Season Ticket Study: The Sunk Cost Fallacy - Researchers sold season theatre tickets at full price, at a discount, or at a bigger discount.
The Checkbox That Saves Lives: The Default Effect - Researchers compared organ donation rates across European countries.
The Discounted Energy Drink: Price Placebo - Researchers gave students the same energy drink and told them it improves mental performance.
The Confident Beginners: Dunning Kruger Effect - In 1999, psychologists Dunning and Kruger tested students on logic, grammar, and humour.
The Embarrassing T-Shirt: The Spotlight Effect - Psychologist Thomas Gilovich had students wear a large Barry Manilow T-shirt they found embarrassing into a room.
The Missing Bullet Holes: Survivorship Bias - In World War Two, the military studied bombers returning from missions and mapped where they had bullet holes.
What Do People Fear?: The Availability Heuristic - Researchers asked people to estimate how often different things cause death.
I Knew It All Along: Hindsight Bias - Before Nixon visited China and Russia in 1972, Baruch Fischhoff asked people to predict possible outcomes.
Words Nobody Could Read: Mere Exposure Effect - Psychologist Robert Zajonc showed people meaningless words and Chinese-like symbols.
The Room Filling With Smoke: Social Proof Of Calm - Latané and Darley had students fill out a form while smoke slowly poured into the room.
The Useless Third Option: The Decoy Effect - Dan Ariely offered students a web only subscription, a print only subscription, and a print plus web bundle.
Why You Love What You Build: The IKEA Effect - Researchers asked people to assemble Ikea boxes, and fold origami, and then say how much they'd pay.
